profesor.texto: Next week we will begin discussing how students prepare for exams. Some research suggests that studying with classmates helps students understand difficult ideas, because they have to explain concepts out loud and answer each other's questions. Other studies find that students who review alone stay more focused and use their time more efficiently. Before our next class, I would like your opinion on this question: When preparing for an important exam, is it better for students to study in a group or by themselves? Why?

estudiantes.texto: I think studying in a group is better. When I prepared for my chemistry exam last semester, my friends explained some problems that I didn't understand in the lecture. Also, it's easier to keep studying for three hours when other people are doing the same thing. When I'm alone, I usually get bored and check my phone.

I prefer studying alone. Groups always spend too much time talking about other things, like weekend plans or the professor's jokes. When I study by myself, I can focus on the topics that I find difficult instead of the ones the group wants to review. I learn more in one hour alone than in three hours with friends.

items.modelo: In my opinion, the best approach is to combine both methods, but to start alone. I agree with Mariam that groups can easily lose focus, so students should first review the material by themselves and find out exactly what they don't understand. After that, a short group session becomes much more useful. For example, before my statistics final last year, I spent two days working through practice problems on my own and wrote down every question I couldn't solve. Then I met two classmates for just one hour, and we only discussed those questions. It was the most efficient review I have ever done. Kevin is right that explaining ideas out loud helps, but that only works when everyone arrives prepared. A study group should be the last step, not the first.
items.notas: El modelo no elige un bando sin más: propone un orden (primero solo, después en grupo), que es una idea nueva que ninguno de los dos compañeros planteó. Cita a Mariam y a Kevin para coincidir en parte con cada uno, y sostiene la postura con un ejemplo personal con detalles (dos días, una hora, solo las dudas). Frase útil: «X is right that…, but…».

profesor.texto: In this unit, we have been looking at how communities change over time. In the past, many people knew their neighbors well because they shopped at the same local stores and spent time outside together. Today, many neighborhoods have online groups where residents share news, sell used items, and organize events. I'd like to hear your view on this question: Has technology made neighbors more connected to each other, or has it made them more isolated?

estudiantes.texto: I believe technology has brought neighbors closer. In my building, we have a group chat with almost every family. When my grandmother needed help carrying groceries, a neighbor I had never met offered to help after reading my message. Without the chat, we would still be strangers who only say hello in the elevator.

I disagree. Online groups give people the feeling that they belong to a community, but they rarely meet in person. In my neighborhood, people complain about parking or noise in the group, but nobody organizes anything face to face. Real connection needs time together, and screens can't replace that.

items.modelo: I think technology can make neighbors more connected, but only when it leads to meetings in real life. Mateo makes a good point that complaining online is not the same as having a community. However, the problem is not the technology itself; it is how people use it. For example, in my neighborhood, someone used our online group to suggest a monthly cleanup of the small park near the bus stop. At first only six people came, but now around thirty neighbors join every month, and many of us stay afterward to have coffee together. I would never have met most of them without that message. So, in my view, online groups work best as a tool for organizing activities, not as a replacement for them. Used that way, technology can actually help rebuild the local connections that we lost.
items.notas: La postura aparece en la primera oración y tiene un matiz claro («but only when…»). El modelo reconoce el argumento de Mateo y lo reencuadra: el problema no es la tecnología sino el uso, que es la idea nueva. El ejemplo tiene cifras concretas (seis personas, luego treinta). Fíjese en «actually», que significa «en realidad», no «actualmente».

profesor.texto: Several companies have recently experimented with a four-day workweek, in which employees work the same total number of hours over four longer days instead of five. Supporters say the extra day off reduces stress and increases loyalty. Critics argue that ten-hour days are exhausting and that customers expect businesses to be available five days a week. For this week's discussion, please explain your reasoning on the following question: Should more companies adopt a four-day workweek with longer days, or should they keep the traditional five-day schedule?

estudiantes.texto: I support the four-day week. My cousin's company switched last year, and she says people now make fewer mistakes because they come back on Monday truly rested. The company also saves money on electricity when the office is closed on Fridays. Happier employees are less likely to quit, which reduces hiring costs.

I think the traditional schedule is still better. Working ten hours in a row is tiring, and most people lose concentration in the last few hours, so the quality of their work drops. Also, many clients need answers on Fridays. If a business is closed that day, customers may simply go to a competitor.

items.modelo: From my perspective, the four-day week is a promising idea, but it should not be adopted in the same way by every company. Olivia raises a valid concern about customers, yet that problem can be solved by rotating days off. For instance, a team of ten people could be split so that half of them rest on Mondays and the other half on Fridays, which keeps the business open five days while every employee still gets a long weekend. What worries me more is the type of work involved. Ten-hour days might be fine for someone answering emails, but they could be risky in jobs that require constant attention, such as operating heavy machinery. Therefore, I believe companies should introduce the schedule gradually, starting with office roles, and measure both productivity and error rates before extending it to everyone.
items.notas: El modelo responde a la objeción de Olivia con una solución concreta (rotar los días libres) y luego aporta un criterio nuevo que nadie mencionó: el tipo de trabajo. Usa conectores de nivel B2 que muestran razonamiento (yet, which, Therefore) y cierra con una recomendación práctica. Estructura útil: «What worries me more is…» para introducir su propia idea.

profesor.texto: Households use a large share of a city's energy, so researchers are looking for ways to encourage people to use less. One approach is to give families detailed information, such as a monthly report comparing their electricity use with that of similar homes nearby. Another approach is to offer financial rewards, like a discount on the bill for reducing consumption. Which strategy do you think would be more effective in changing people's long-term habits: providing information or offering money? Why?

estudiantes.texto: I think financial rewards work better. People are busy, and most of them will ignore a report full of numbers. But if they know they can save twenty dollars a month, they will turn off lights and unplug devices. Money is a clear and immediate reason to change, and everyone understands it.

I would choose information. Rewards only work while they last; when the discount ends, people go back to their old habits. A comparison with neighbors creates a little friendly competition. Nobody wants to be the family that uses twice as much energy as the house next door.

items.modelo: I agree with Samir that information is the better long-term strategy, although I would add that the way it is presented matters a lot. Rachel is right that many people ignore pages of numbers, so the report has to be simple and personal. For example, instead of saying that a family used 450 kilowatt-hours, it could point out that their air conditioner alone costs as much as a weekly trip to the grocery store. When my family received a message like that last summer, we started setting the temperature two degrees higher, and we still do it today even though nobody pays us for it. That shows the main weakness of rewards: they teach people to save energy for the money, not because they understand their own consumption. Once people clearly see where their energy goes, the change tends to last.
items.notas: El modelo elige postura de inmediato, pero toma lo válido del argumento contrario (Rachel tiene razón en que nadie lee números) y lo convierte en una condición nueva: el informe debe ser simple y personal. El ejemplo familiar prueba la idea central, que el hábito sigue sin dinero de por medio. Frase útil: «although I would add that…».

profesor.texto: Many cities have closed some downtown streets to cars and turned them into pedestrian-only zones with benches, trees, and outdoor cafés. Supporters say these changes make city centers more pleasant and help local shops. Opponents argue that they make it harder for delivery trucks, older residents, and people who have difficulty walking to reach the area. Please explain your position: Should cities convert their main downtown streets into pedestrian-only zones, or should cars continue to have access?

estudiantes.texto: I think pedestrian zones are a great idea. When my city closed two blocks of the main avenue, the area became much livelier. Families started walking there on weekends, and new restaurants opened. Fewer cars also means less noise and cleaner air, which benefits everyone who lives and works downtown.

I'm against closing streets completely. My grandfather can't walk long distances, and when cars were banned near his favorite market, he stopped going. Some shop owners also lost customers who used to stop by quickly in their cars. Cities should reduce traffic, but not eliminate it.

items.modelo: In my view, cities should create pedestrian zones, but they need to design them carefully so that nobody is left out. Aiko describes a real problem: if a market becomes hard to reach, older people may simply stop going. However, I don't think the solution is to keep cars on the street. A better option would be a small electric shuttle that runs every ten minutes from nearby parking areas to the center of the zone. For example, the historic center of a city I visited last year has this kind of service, and I saw many elderly residents and parents with strollers using it. Deliveries could also be limited to early mornings, before the shops open. With measures like these, cities could keep the benefits Felix mentions, such as cleaner air and busier restaurants, while making the area accessible to everyone.
items.notas: El modelo apoya las zonas peatonales sin ignorar la objeción de Aiko: la acepta como real y propone dos medidas nuevas (un bus eléctrico y horarios de entrega). Al final retoma a Felix para mostrar que su propuesta conserva las ventajas de ambos lados. Estructura útil: «A better option would be…» para presentar una alternativa.

profesor.texto: This week we are studying how people make decisions. Some psychologists believe that our first feeling about a choice, sometimes called intuition, is often surprisingly accurate. Others argue that we make better decisions when we slow down, list the advantages and disadvantages, and take time to think. Consider an important choice, such as which university to attend or which job to accept. Is it better to trust your first feeling, or to analyze the decision carefully over a long period? Why?

estudiantes.texto: I think it is better to trust your first feeling. When I chose my apartment, I felt comfortable the moment I walked in, even though another one was cheaper. Two years later, I still love living there. If you think for too long, you can get confused and lose good opportunities.

I believe careful analysis is better for important decisions. Feelings can change from one day to the next, especially when we are tired or stressed. When I chose my university, I compared costs, courses, and distance from home in a table. That helped me avoid an expensive mistake.

items.modelo: I agree with Javier that important decisions need careful thinking, but I believe our feelings should be part of that process too. A list of advantages and disadvantages is useful because it helps us see facts that we might ignore when we are excited. However, Nina's example shows that a strong feeling can also contain useful information. For example, when I was choosing between two part-time jobs last year, one offered better pay, and my list clearly said that I should take it. But during the interview, the manager was rude to another employee, and I felt uncomfortable. I chose the other job, and I'm glad I did, because the team is very friendly. So I think the best method is to analyze the options first and then ask yourself how you honestly feel about the result.
items.notas: El modelo combina las dos posturas en un método nuevo (analizar primero y después consultar la intuición), y lo demuestra con una historia corta y clara. Usa estructuras de nivel B1 bien controladas (when, because, but, so) y menciona a los dos compañeros. Recuerde que en inglés el sujeto nunca se omite: «I'm glad I did», no «Am glad».

profesor.texto: More and more people now follow the news through short videos that last less than a minute. These videos are easy to share and can reach young audiences who rarely read newspapers. However, some researchers worry that such short formats leave out important context and make complex issues seem simpler than they are. Please support your answer to this question: Are short news videos a good way for people to stay informed, or do they reduce the public's understanding of current events?

estudiantes.texto: Short videos are a positive development. Many of my friends never read the news before, but now they watch quick summaries every morning. Even if a video doesn't explain everything, it makes people aware of what's happening, and they can look for more details later if a topic interests them.

I think short videos do more harm than good. In sixty seconds, a creator can only show one side of a story, and viewers often believe they fully understand it. I have seen friends argue strongly about a topic after watching one clip, without knowing basic facts about it.

items.modelo: I can see why Chloe is optimistic, but I mostly agree with Omar, and I think the real danger is not the length of the videos but the way they are recommended. Apps usually show people more of whatever they already watch, so a short clip rarely leads to a longer article; it leads to another short clip. For instance, last month I watched one video about planned changes to the bus routes in my city, and for the next week my feed showed me dozens of similar videos, almost all repeating the same complaint. I never saw a detailed explanation until a professor mentioned the topic in class. In my opinion, short videos could still be useful if they always included a link to a full report, but without that, they make people feel informed while actually giving them less information.
items.notas: El modelo toma partido, pero desplaza la discusión hacia una causa que ninguno mencionó: los sistemas de recomendación. El ejemplo personal muestra el efecto con claridad y el cierre propone una condición concreta (enlazar el informe completo). Estructura útil: «the real danger is not X but Y» para presentar una idea nueva.

profesor.texto: Public health campaigns try to change everyday behavior, such as encouraging people to sleep more, exercise regularly, or wash their hands. Designers of these campaigns face a basic choice. Some messages emphasize the risks of unhealthy habits, for example by describing the problems caused by lack of sleep. Others focus on the benefits of healthy habits, such as having more energy or a better mood. In your view, and for what reasons, which approach is more effective at producing lasting changes in behavior: emphasizing risks or emphasizing benefits?

estudiantes.texto: Messages about risk are more powerful. People tend to ignore advice until they understand what they could lose. When my university posted information about how lack of sleep damages memory before exams, many students I know changed their routines. A clear warning creates a sense of urgency that positive messages usually lack.

I believe benefits work better over time. Warnings can make people anxious, and anxious people often avoid the topic instead of changing. My gym's campaign focused on how exercise improves mood and sleep, and attendance increased for months. People keep a habit when it makes them feel good, not when they are afraid.

items.modelo: While Elena is right that warnings capture attention, I would argue that they rarely sustain change on their own. Fear works as a starting point, but once the initial alarm fades, people need a reason to continue that feels rewarding rather than threatening. That is why I think the most effective campaigns move deliberately from risks to benefits. A good example is a sleep campaign my university ran last year. The first posters, put up just before midterms, explained how staying up all night impairs memory. A few weeks later, however, the messages shifted to students describing how much more productive they felt after sleeping seven hours. Several friends told me the first message made them try, but the second made them stay. In other words, the choice Dr. Lindgren presents may be a false one: timing matters as much as content.
items.notas: Es una respuesta de nivel C1 porque no se queda en «riesgos» o «beneficios»: cuestiona la pregunta misma y propone que el orden en el tiempo es lo decisivo. Concede a Elena con «While…», desarrolla un ejemplo en dos fases y cierra con una frase memorable («the first message made them try, but the second made them stay»). Vocabulario preciso: sustain change, initial alarm fades, deliberately.
